content: In 2020, the World Health Organization (WHO) classified Pakistan as a high tuberculosis (TB) burden country, with an incidence rate of 259 cases per 100,000 people. Smoking was estimated to contribute to 53,000 TB cases among men and 3,600 cases among women in the same year. Smoking not only increases the risk of developing TB but also worsens treatment outcomes and doubles the risk of TB-related mortality. To address this, Pakistan developed a tailored smoking cessation intervention for TB patients through a collaboration between the national TB program and the University of York. This intervention involved brief, 8-minute behavioral support sessions delivered by regular TB program staff. These sessions provided information on TB, healthy behaviors, and strategies to quit smoking. Following a three-year trial called the TB & Tobacco trial, healthcare workers were interviewed to optimize the intervention before scaling it up. Based on their feedback, the recording and reporting systems were revised to document smoking status at registration and treatment completion, training was condensed to a half-day, and provincial TB program leads were engaged. The trial demonstrated that 25% of TB patients successfully quit smoking, as verified by self-reported abstinence and biochemical testing at 6 and 12 months. Those who quit smoking showed better TB treatment outcomes, including higher sputum conversion rates, greater treatment success, and lower relapse rates compared to those who continued smoking. The intervention was subsequently scaled up in 59 out of 121 health facilities in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Province, encompassing urban, rural, private, and public centers. Key factors for success included close collaboration between researchers and national/provincial programs to evaluate the intervention's effectiveness and impact on TB treatment outcomes. Organizational commitment was evident through joint funding of the intervention. Consultations with healthcare workers helped identify ways to improve feasibility and acceptability for broader implementation. Primary health care (PHC), which provides integrated, comprehensive, and affordable services, is a cornerstone of universal health coverage (UHC). Programs should aim to decentralize and integrate TB and comorbidity services at the primary care level. Countries may need to prioritize actions on TB and comorbidities based on evidence, data reviews, root cause analyses, and stakeholder consultations. WHO's people-centered framework for TB program planning and prioritization offers guidance for tailoring services to the needs and preferences of affected individuals while minimizing time and financial burdens for accessing care. Collaborative action on TB and comorbidities can improve overall health outcomes, enhance resource efficiency, and promote integrated, patient-centered services. Planning should align with national health strategies, health system strengthening efforts, and UHC goals. Key areas for planning include quality-assured health services, a well-trained workforce, functional information systems, equitable access to essential medicines and technologies, sustainable health financing, and strong leadership and governance. Models of care for TB and comorbidities range from standalone services to fully integrated one-stop-shop approaches. Standalone services may involve screening for TB or comorbidities and referring patients for diagnosis and treatment. While simple and cost-effective, this model often requires patients to attend multiple appointments at different locations, increasing the risk of loss to follow-up and financial strain. Co-located services, where separate providers operate in the same or adjacent premises, reduce travel and enable better integration but may still be time-consuming and costly for patients. Fully integrated models provide collaborative services for TB and comorbidities in a single location, often on the same day, by the same healthcare worker. These models reduce transportation costs, income loss, and logistical challenges while simplifying record-keeping and improving time efficiency. However, transitioning to such models requires alignment of financing, human resources, multidisciplinary training, and infrastructure investment. Infection prevention and control (IPC) measures are critical to prevent nosocomial TB transmission, but concerns about transmission should not hinder integration, as early detection and treatment in integrated settings may reduce TB risk compared to separate services. In Georgia, an integrated model of screening and care for TB, HIV, and viral hepatitis was introduced in 2018 in the Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti region, which has a higher burden of these diseases compared to the national average. This model aimed to improve diagnosis and management at the primary care level, particularly among high-risk groups such as prisoners and people who inject drugs.
